fields.m.setting: General education fourth grade with a resource room; campus with an open courtyard; 1 para shared across two classes
fields.m.beh: Elopement: leaving the assigned area (classroom, line, table) without permission by more than 3 m, or leaving the building; includes running to the courtyard or the parking-lot fence. Not: moving to a permitted station.
fields.m.eadesign: trial-based FA in the classroom plus a tangible (courtyard) test, 3 series (EA-1, 9/9–9/18); escape from reading tasks and access to the courtyard both differentiated
fields.m.reinf: Escape from reading-group demands and access to the courtyard (outdoor play), each confirmed; EO strongest in the hour before recess and during round-robin reading.
fields.m.prec: Looks at the door, puts materials in the desk, asks 'what time is it?'.
fields.m.repdesc: Asks for a break in the resource room only; no way to ask for the courtyard.
fields.m.pref: PA-1 (MSWO, 9/4): courtyard time > scooter board > drawing > helper job.
fields.m.curr: Reading is two grades below placement; round-robin reading aloud is the hardest demand.
fields.m.constraints: Doors cannot be locked from inside; the courtyard gate to the parking lot is 40 m from her class; one para shared.
fields.m.safety: Reached the parking-lot fence twice in September; a safety plan (CR-1) exists; no injuries.
fields.sel.why: From the model's questions; see the rationale on each card.
fields.cp[0].s0: Assess the curricular variables associated with the behavior: difficulty relative to current skills, task length, functional versus arbitrary tasks, preference, novelty.
fields.cp[0].s1: Assess the instructional variables: session length, massed versus interspersed trials, prompting method, trial rate, density of positive reinforcement during work.
fields.cp[0].s2: Revise: teach prerequisite skills before advanced ones; shorten sessions; intersperse easy and mastered tasks; use the prompting method the student tolerates.
fields.cp[0].s3: Increase positive reinforcement for compliance and task completion during instruction (denser than any break contingency).
fields.cp[0].s4: Re-evaluate the behavior under the revised curriculum before adding consequence-based components.
fields.cp[1].s0: Define the existing appropriate request (vocal, sign, gesture) that will produce the reinforcer.
fields.cp[1].s1: Reinforce every occurrence of the request under the EO with the functional reinforcer immediately.
fields.cp[1].s2: Withhold the reinforcer for problem behavior; if withholding is not feasible, arrange longer, higher-quality, and more immediate reinforcement for the request than problem behavior obtains (Athens & Vollmer, 2010).
fields.cp[1].s3: Watch for a temporary increase in problem behavior when a pre-existing response is reinforced (Derby et al., 1998, as reviewed by Tiger et al., 2008).
fields.cp[1].s4: Thin as for FCT once the request is reliable.
fields.cp[2].s0: Set the initial delivery interval below the mean baseline interresponse time (dense; near-continuous for severe behavior; Hagopian et al., 1994).
fields.cp[2].s1: Deliver the reinforcer (attention or the item) at each interval end regardless of behavior; keep the delivery brief and consistent.
fields.cp[2].s2: Withhold the reinforcer contingent on problem behavior (extinction) where feasible; delay a scheduled delivery briefly if problem behavior immediately precedes it.
fields.cp[2].s3: Thin the interval by steps when the criterion is met, toward a terminal schedule the setting can sustain.
fields.cp[2].s4: Introduce FCT after thinning rather than during a rich NCR schedule (Goh et al., 2000).
fields.cp[3].s0: Write a schedule of brief positive attention (e.g., 10 s of specific praise or conversation every 5 min) delivered by any adult in the room regardless of behavior.
fields.cp[3].s1: Set the interval below the baseline mean interresponse time at first; use a timer or app so delivery does not depend on the behavior.
fields.cp[3].s2: If the behavior occurs just before a scheduled delivery, delay it briefly.
fields.cp[3].s3: Thin the schedule as the behavior stays low; do not run a rich schedule at the same time as FCT acquisition (Goh, Iwata, & DeLeon, 2000).
fields.cp[4].s0: Before the routine in which the behavior occurs, provide free access to the maintaining reinforcer (attention or the item) for a set period.
fields.cp[4].s1: Begin the routine immediately after; expect lower value of the reinforcer and less behavior for a limited window.
fields.cp[4].s2: Record the length of the effect and adjust timing; combine with the consequence components rather than relying on it alone.
fields.cp[5].s0: Identify high-p and low-p instructions from caregiver and staff nominations, then test each on 10 probe trials in random order: high-p = cooperation on at least 80% of trials, low-p = under 40% (the operational definitions of Lemons & Wilder, 2026); build a pool of at least six single-step, brief high-p instructions on the Antecedents sheet planner.
fields.cp[5].s1: Deliver 3 high-p instructions 1–3 s apart (the next immediately after cooperation) with brief praise for each; deliver the low-p instruction within 3 s of cooperation with the third, and only after cooperation with all three (study values, not tested optima).
fields.cp[5].s2: Order: varied (a different order each trial, never the previous trial's order) unless a brief probe preassessment shows a constant order is equal or better (Lemons & Wilder, 2026 recommendation); if constant, write the fixed order.
fields.cp[5].s3: If a high-p instruction is not cooperated with: pause 30 s and restart a new 3-instruction sequence; do not deliver the low-p instruction. Score cooperation as initiation within 10 s.
fields.cp[5].s4: Reinforce low-p cooperation per the plan (praise in the study; the authors suggest higher-quality reinforcement in practice); the consequence for low-p noncooperation comes from the Responding sheet by function; fade the number of high-p requests as cooperation holds.
fields.cp[6].s0: Intersperse mastered, easy items among difficult ones (e.g., 3 easy : 1 hard) during instruction.
fields.cp[6].s1: Praise each correct easy item; keep the pace brisk.
fields.cp[6].s2: Adjust the ratio from the behavior data; reduce interspersal as tolerance grows.
fields.cp[7].s0: Present instruction at a brisk pace with short response intervals; avoid long waits between items.
fields.cp[7].s1: Keep work periods short (e.g., 5 min) with a scheduled break, lengthening as the behavior stays low.
fields.cp[7].s2: Use the student's preferred and functional tasks where the curriculum allows.
fields.cp[8].s0: Prepare 3–4 task sets at the student's instructional level.
fields.cp[8].s1: Before each work period present the array and let the student choose the order (or the timing) of tasks.
fields.cp[8].s2: When one task is complete, offer the remaining tasks again.
fields.cp[8].s3: Pair with a consequence component (extinction or DNRA) because choice alone programs no consequence for problem behavior.
fields.cp[8].s4: Record choice made, task completed, and problem behavior per period.
fields.cp[9].s0: Provide a visual or picture activity schedule the student manipulates (check off, move a card) as each activity ends.
fields.cp[9].s1: Give an advance notice before transitions (e.g., 2-min and 30-s warnings) and a consistent transition signal.
fields.cp[9].s2: Preview any change to the routine at the start of the day; keep the order stable where possible.
fields.cp[9].s3: For transition-evoked behavior, combine with the function-based component identified on EA-1 (Wilder et al., 2006).
fields.cp[10].s0: Preview the next day's or next period's materials in a low-demand, preferred context (with a parent or aide) before the lesson.
fields.cp[10].s1: Keep priming brief and reinforcing; do not test.
fields.cp[10].s2: Track performance and problem behavior in the primed lessons versus unprimed ones.
fields.cp[11].s0: Identify from the SP-1 and ABC-1 data which peers, locations, and materials precede the behavior.
fields.cp[11].s1: Seat the student away from evocative peers and doorways (or near the exit route when elopement is the target and a staff member sits between), with materials within reach and the break area visible.
fields.cp[11].s2: Use row seating for independent work; rearrange only after data show a problem with the current arrangement.
fields.cp[11].s3: Review the arrangement at each plan review.
fields.cp[12].s0: At arrival, check the setting events the assessment identified (sleep, illness, allergy symptoms, missed medication, conflict on the bus or at home, hunger) with the parent note or a brief check.
fields.cp[12].s1: When a setting event is present, run the neutralizing routine: a preferred activity first, reduced or shortened demands, extra noncontingent attention, and choice for that morning (Horner et al., 1997).
fields.cp[12].s2: Record the setting event and the routine used on the data sheet; report medical setting events to the nurse.
fields.cp[13].s0: Identify the specific social consequence the student prefers (form of praise, tickles, conversation, high five) with a social-interaction preference assessment (Smaby et al., 2007; Call et al., 2013).
fields.cp[13].s1: Deliver it immediately and enthusiastically for the target response; keep it brief.
fields.cp[13].s2: Test it under intermittent schedules before relying on it; if it weakens, back it with tangibles or tokens.
fields.cp[14].s0: Completing a unit schedule (e.g., FR 3 correct) earns a token; completing the exchange schedule (e.g., 5 tokens) earns the backup reinforcer.
fields.cp[14].s1: Establish tokens by pairing with immediate exchange at first (exchange after 1 token), then lengthen the exchange requirement.
fields.cp[14].s2: Offer a menu of backup reinforcers to limit satiation; keep the exchange schedule dense enough to contact the backup daily.
fields.cp[14].s3: Thin the unit schedule before the exchange schedule.
fields.cp[15].s0: Line up 5–7 items; the student approaches one and receives brief access; remove it and re-present the rest until all are chosen or 30 s passes without a choice.
fields.cp[15].s1: Repeat 3–5 times; rank by mean selection order or percentage.
fields.cp[15].s2: Use the brief version before sessions to track daily shifts (DeLeon et al., 2001).
fields.cp[16].s0: Reinforce every occurrence of the target response during acquisition.
fields.cp[16].s1: Hold CRF until the response is independent and stable.
fields.cp[16].s2: Thin only by a planned schedule (see the thinning ladder).
fields.cp[17].s0: Begin with the prompt that guarantees the response (e.g., full physical), delivered immediately with the instruction.
fields.cp[17].s1: Reduce to the next less intrusive level after the criterion (e.g., 3 consecutive correct); return one level after 2 errors.
fields.cp[17].s2: Reinforce prompted responses during acquisition; differentially reinforce unprompted responses once they appear.
fields.cp[17].s3: Use when errors evoke problem behavior or the response is new.
fields.cp[18].s0: Begin with a 0-s delay between instruction and prompt; increase the delay in small steps (e.g., 1 s per session or per criterion) as unprompted responses appear.
fields.cp[18].s1: Transfer of control is shown when the learner responds before the prompt; keep the terminal delay short enough to prevent errors.
fields.cp[18].s2: Reinforce unprompted responses more richly than prompted ones.
fields.cp[19].s0: In every teaching trial deliver the instruction and the controlling prompt together (0-s delay).
fields.cp[19].s1: Run daily probe trials without the prompt to measure acquisition; probes are the only unprompted opportunities.
fields.cp[19].s2: Use when errors must be near zero and probes can be scheduled.
fields.cp[20].s0: Compare candidate prompt types (vocal, model, physical) or hierarchies (MTL vs LTM) on equivalent skill sets in an alternating-treatments design.
fields.cp[20].s1: Select the procedure that produced the fastest acquisition with the fewest errors and least problem behavior.
fields.cp[20].s2: Re-run when a new response class is introduced.
fields.cp[21].s0: After an error, model or deliver the correct response, then re-present the instruction and require an independent (or least-prompted) correct response before moving on.
fields.cp[21].s1: Reinforce the corrected response with praise only; reserve the token or item for unprompted responses.
fields.cp[22].s0: Begin in the synthesized-test context from the analysis: present the establishing operations together (e.g., demand + item removal + diverted attention).
fields.cp[22].s1: Teach a simple FCR that produces the synthesized reinforcers (e.g., a card or "my way"); prompt at the EO and reinforce every response for 30–60 s of the reinforcers; withhold reinforcers for problem behavior.
fields.cp[22].s2: When the simple FCR is independent, teach the complex FCR: gain attention, then a polite, complete request ("Excuse me. May I have my way, please?"); reinforce only the complex form once acquired.
fields.cp[22].s3: Keep sessions short and end on reinforcement; problem behavior during acquisition is addressed by re-presenting the EO and prompting the FCR.
fields.cp[23].s0: Once the complex FCR is reliable, deny it on a small proportion of trials ("No, not right now") and immediately prompt a tolerance response ("Okay") or an acknowledgment gesture; reinforce the tolerance response with the synthesized reinforcers at first.
fields.cp[23].s1: Increase the proportion of denials gradually (e.g., 10% → 25% → 50% → 90%; in Hanley et al., 2014, three of every five FCRs met a delay or denial) while the FCR is still honored on the rest; keep denial unpredictable.
fields.cp[23].s2: If problem behavior follows a denial, withhold the reinforcers, re-present the EO, and prompt the FCR and tolerance response again.
fields.cp[23].s3: Record FCRs, tolerance responses, and problem behavior per session.
fields.cp[24].s0: Begin with the FCR honored immediately; introduce a signaled delay of a few seconds, then lengthen it stepwise (e.g., 5 → 15 → 30 → 60 s → several minutes) as problem behavior stays low.
fields.cp[24].s1: During the delay, prompt and reinforce engagement in an alternative activity or work (the delay is filled, not empty).
fields.cp[24].s2: Add unpredictable denials with the tolerance response once delays are tolerated.
fields.cp[24].s3: Step back one level after two sessions with problem behavior during the delay.
fields.cp[25].s0: After the tolerance response, present one contextually appropriate behavior (relinquish the item, transition, or complete one instruction) before the synthesized reinforcers are delivered.
fields.cp[25].s1: Lengthen the chain and vary its content unpredictably (one instruction → three → a short task → a full routine) while keeping some trials in which the FCR is honored immediately.
fields.cp[25].s2: Reinforce the chain with the synthesized reinforcers at a decreasing but unpredictable probability; add praise throughout.
fields.cp[25].s3: Extend to new implementers and settings with the same sequence; probe the natural routine before and after.
fields.cp[26].s0: Assess the current mand: does it occur only after a vocal prompt or the item in view (prompt or stimulus control) or under the EO alone?
fields.cp[26].s1: Fade the prompt and the visible item with a time delay so the mand occurs in the absence of both.
fields.cp[26].s2: For sign or picture mands, pair the vocal model and reinforce vocal approximations to move toward vocal mands (Carbone et al., 2010).
fields.cp[27].s0: Capture naturally occurring EOs during routines (snack, play, transitions); pause and wait for the mand before providing the item or action.
fields.cp[27].s1: Prompt only as needed, fade quickly, and reinforce with the item requested.
fields.cp[27].s2: Rotate across settings, listeners, and items to build generalized manding; record mands per hour in the natural routine.
fields.cp[28].s0: Before the activity, have the student state what they will do ("I will use the break card if the work is hard"); reinforce the statement at first (reinforce-saying phase).
fields.cp[28].s1: Shift reinforcement to correspondence: reinforce only when the stated behavior occurs (reinforce-correspondence phase); use say-then-do ordering (Israel & O'Leary, 1973).
fields.cp[28].s2: Fade to intermittent checks and to the student's own review of correspondence.
fields.cp[28].s3: Use when the student can state a plan and the goal is self-management across settings.
fields.cp[29].s0: Score the relevant modules (basic living, home, community participation, school, vocational, independent living).
fields.cp[29].s1: Select functional skills the replacement behavior will make possible (e.g., requesting help during a chore).
fields.cp[29].s2: Teach with the prompting and error-correction procedures chosen on the prompting sheet; track independence per skill.
fields.cp[30].p2: CR-1 elopement plan: if she passes the courtyard gate, radio the office, two adults to the parking-lot fence, parent call.
fields.cp[30].s0: On the precursor: At the look to the door or "what time is it?": prompt the break card or the courtyard card ("courtyard after reading"), honor the break at once; the courtyard request earns the next scheduled courtyard time.
fields.cp[30].s1: On the target behavior: Follow at a walking pace, keep her in sight, do not chase or call out; when she stops, prompt the card; walk back together; the reading task resumes where it stopped (escape extinction); the courtyard is not entered after elopement.
fields.cp[30].s2: After the episode: Record the episode, where she went, and the antecedent on DD-1; check the gate was closed.
fields.cp[30].s3: Staff do not: Do not chase, grab, or lock doors; do not cancel the scheduled courtyard time as a punishment; do not send her to the office.
fields.cp[30].s4: Record the episode, the step used, and whether the reinforcer was contacted (integrity error).
fields.cp[30].s5: Crisis procedure applies only when the safety trigger is met and is documented separately.
fields.cp[31].bsrc: Answering a cell phone and handing a help card to a store employee when separated from staff in the community (Hoch et al., 2009)
fields.cp[31].p0: when the phone rings: answer it, follow the phone instruction to find an adult, say 'I'm lost' or 'Help me', hand over the help card, and wait with the adult until staff arrive
fields.cp[31].p2: total task; one phone call is one trial (5 trials per session at school, 1 per session in the community)
fields.cp[31].p3: at school a second adult gives full physical prompts, moves to partial prompts after 3 to 5 trials, then delays the prompt in 2-s steps (0, 2, 4 s) and fades distance until out of view; in the community, staff come into view only when a step is missed and give least-to-most prompts, then step back
fields.cp[31].p4: 100% correct on 2 consecutive sessions at each training stage
fields.cp[31].p5: praise plus a preferred food given discreetly on reunion; tokens or food start on FR 1, move to VR 2 and are thinned in 2-response steps until only praise remains
fields.cp[31].p6: percentage of the 5 chain responses done correctly per call
fields.cp[31].ta:
Answering the phone and getting help when lost:
1. Answer the ringing cell phone
2. Follow the caller's directions to find an adult
3. Tell the adult 'I'm lost' or 'Help me' (a close try counts)
4. Hand the help card and the phone to the adult
5. Wait with the adult until the parent or teacher arrives
fields.cp[31].s0: Give the student his or her own cell phone to carry on a belt or in a pocket, plus a pocket-sized card stating that the student is lost and cannot speak, with name and diagnosis, and asking the reader to take the phone and listen to the teacher or parent.
fields.cp[31].s1: At school, call the student's phone from different places in the building while a second adult prompts the student to take out the phone, press talk and say 'hello'.
fields.cp[31].s2: Give a simple direction over the phone and, if it is not followed within 5 seconds, have the second adult guide the student, moving from full to partial physical prompts after 3 to 5 trials and then delaying the prompt by 0, 2, then 4 seconds.
fields.cp[31].s3: When directions are followed at 100% for 2 sessions, tell the student on the phone to find an adult and give the card, while the second adult prompts the student to approach an adult, say 'I'm lost' or 'Help me', and hand over the card.
fields.cp[31].s4: Fade those prompts from most to least and move the second adult farther away until out of view, until the student is correct on all 5 trials in 2 consecutive sessions.
fields.cp[31].s5: Reinforce each correct chain with praise and a preferred food or token (discreetly on reunion in the community), on FR 1 at first, then VR 2, thinning by 2 responses until only praise is given.
fields.cp[31].s6: In stores the student visits often, step out of sight while a second staff member keeps the student in view at all times, and call if the student has not sought help within 1 minute.
fields.cp[31].s7: If the phone is not answered by the third ring or a step is missed, come into view, give least-to-most prompts for that step, and back away again.
fields.cp[31].s8: Teach the student to go to an employee at a counter or register and hand over the card alone, offering the phone only when asked; when the employee takes the phone, ask the employee to keep the student there and to tell you the location.
fields.cp[31].s9: Probe untrained stores with no prompts or rewards, and run 1 to 3 booster sessions at training stores whenever accuracy falls below 80%.
fields.cp[31].data: Percentage of the 5 chain responses done correctly per call (answer, follow the instruction to find an adult, say the help phrase, hand over the card, wait), plus whether the community adult took the card, spoke with staff and waited with the student, recorded on Form DD-1.
fields.cp[31].mat: Student's own cell phone; 3 x 5 inch printed help card kept in a pocket; staff phone; preferred foods or the student's token board; a second staff member to keep the student in sight at all times.
fields.cp[32].bsrc: Functional communication training with extinction and gradual, signaled schedule thinning (practice guide) (Tiger et al., 2008)
fields.cp[32].p0: a low-effort response that unfamiliar people will recognize and the student can learn fast, such as a picture exchange, a single sign, a voice-output button or a short vocal request; an existing response such as signing 'all done' can be strengthened; make it more complex once problem behavior is low
fields.cp[32].p1: most-to-least (physical prompt as soon as the motivating situation is set up, then faded in intensity) or least-to-most with a delay (wait about 5 s, then a vocal or physical prompt, with the delay lengthened over trials)
fields.cp[32].p2: the reinforcer found in the functional analysis, given every time at first; if extinction cannot be used, make reinforcement for the communication longer, better, faster or more frequent than for problem behavior
fields.cp[32].p3: withhold the maintaining reinforcer after problem behavior from the start of treatment
fields.cp[32].p4: lengthen a delay to reinforcement starting at 1 s with a signal that it is coming; or alternate signaled periods when requests are and are not honored (for example two colored cards); for escape, raise the amount of work required before a break request is honored
fields.cp[32].p5: a schedule caregivers can keep up; the guide cites success with requests honored only during signaled periods covering about 20% of the time
fields.cp[32].s0: Confirm the maintaining reinforcer with a functional analysis before starting.
fields.cp[32].s1: Pick a communication response that is low effort, easy for unfamiliar people to recognize, and quick to learn.
fields.cp[32].s2: Begin with a trained interventionist in a safe, controlled setting and create many practice opportunities by setting up the motivating situation (remove the item, withhold attention, or present the task).
fields.cp[32].s3: Prompt the communication response either right away (most-to-least) or after a short wait such as 5 s (least-to-most with a delay), and fade the prompt over trials.
fields.cp[32].s4: Deliver the maintaining reinforcer every time the student communicates during initial training.
fields.cp[32].s5: Withhold the maintaining reinforcer after problem behavior.
fields.cp[32].s6: Once problem behavior is low, thin reinforcement gradually using a signaled delay starting at 1 s, signaled periods when requests can and cannot be honored, or, for escape, more work before the break request is honored.
fields.cp[32].s7: Offer other preferred items during delays or unavailable periods to compete with problem behavior during thinning.
fields.cp[32].s8: Extend training across several trainers and settings, bring in materials from the classroom, train in each needed setting, and teach caregivers how to respond.
fields.cp[32].s9: Increase the complexity of the communication response over time, for example a full request such as 'May I have ___, please'.
fields.cp[32].data: Rate of problem behavior and of independent communication responses per session, prompt level used, and the current thinning step, plus probes in each setting and with each caregiver, recorded on Form DD-1.
fields.cp[32].mat: Communication materials (picture cards, voice-output device or sign), the reinforcer identified in the functional analysis, signals for reinforcement availability such as colored cards, a timer, and a protected setting for early training.
fields.cp[33].bsrc: Progressive delay fading on a variable-interval schedule after FCT for elopement (Stevenson et al., 2016)
fields.cp[33].p0: VI 15 s, 30 s, 45 s, 90 s, then 300 s; advance after 3 consecutive sessions with no elopement, using preset interval lists (e.g., VI 30 s drew from 5, 10, 15, 30, 35, 40, 45 and 60 s)
fields.cp[33].p2: the adult tells the student the item will have to wait and invites them to keep walking
fields.cp[33].s0: Start delay fading only after FCT has produced steady requests and rare elopement.
fields.cp[33].s1: When the student requests an item or activity, tell the student it has to wait and keep walking together; start the interval timer at that moment.
fields.cp[33].s2: Praise calm walking near the adult while the interval runs.
fields.cp[33].s3: When the interval has ended, give the item or activity for the student's next appropriate request.
fields.cp[33].s4: If the requested item is not available at all, say it is not possible right now and suggest looking for something else on the walk.
fields.cp[33].s5: Draw each interval from the preset list for the current VI value so the wait is unpredictable.
fields.cp[33].s6: Advance to the next VI value (15, 30, 45, 90, then 300 s) after 3 consecutive sessions without elopement.
fields.cp[33].data: Elopements and appropriate requests per 10-min walk, plus the VI value in effect, recorded on Form DD-1.
fields.cp[33].mat: Timer or phone app with preset interval lists for each VI value, data sheet.
fields.ant.chosen: A_NCA, A_PRESESS, A_HIGHP, A_INTERSPERSE, A_PACE, CHOICE, A_SCHEDULE, A_PRIME, A_SEAT, A_SETEVENT
fields.ec.0: no, the prompting procedure is errorless
fields.skb.1: contrived sessions first, then natural routines
fields.sk.chosen: SBT_FCR, SBT_TR, DT_PROG, SBT_CAB, MAND_XFER, MAND_NET, SAYDO, AFLS
fields.rb.prec: At the look to the door or "what time is it?": prompt the break card or the courtyard card ("courtyard after reading"), honor the break at once; the courtyard request earns the next scheduled courtyard time.
fields.rb.target: Follow at a walking pace, keep her in sight, do not chase or call out; when she stops, prompt the card; walk back together; the reading task resumes where it stopped (escape extinction); the courtyard is not entered after elopement.
fields.rb.after: Record the episode, where she went, and the antecedent on DD-1; check the gate was closed.
fields.rb.not: Do not chase, grab, or lock doors; do not cancel the scheduled courtyard time as a punishment; do not send her to the office.
fields.rb.crisis: CR-1 elopement plan: if she passes the courtyard gate, radio the office, two adults to the parking-lot fence, parent call.
fields.p.visit: Weekly 30-minute visit: observe one session, score the integrity checklist, give feedback, model any step under 80%.
fields.p.pre: Probes before the plan starts: the target and the replacement behavior in 3 settings (class, specials, cafeteria) with 2 adults.
fields.p.gen: Train with two adults and in two settings from the first week; the natural cue (the demand itself) is the SD; the card goes with the student.
fields.p.post: Probes in the untrained setting at 2 and 4 weeks after criterion; monthly after.
fields.p.complex: The simple response first; the longer form once the simple one is at criterion.
fields.p.design: Baseline to treatment with the EA-1 treatment sheet; reversal only if the team agrees.
